subject: physics
title: Gravitational fields and Newton's law of gravitation
key_idea: A gravitational field is a region where a mass feels a force because of another mass. Its strength is the force on each kilogram, g = F/m. Newton's law gives the force between point masses, and from it g = GM/r² for a point mass.

blocks.text: This section defines a field, shows how to draw one and defines gravitational field strength.

items.meaning: A region in which a body experiences a non-contact force.
A region in which a mass experiences a force because of another mass.
The force acting per unit mass on a small test mass placed at that point.

items: Gravitational fields are due to objects having **mass**.
The field is a **vector**: it has a size and a direction, the direction a mass would be pulled.
Gravity is a universal force that acts between all matter, and it is always attractive.
Field strength is measured in N/kg, which is the same as m/s².

blocks.label: Gravitational field strength
where: F = gravitational force on the mass (N)
m = the mass in the field (kg)

items: Field lines show the direction of the force on a mass placed in the field.
Arrows point in the direction a mass would move, so they point towards the centre of a planet.
The closer together the lines, the stronger the field.
Around a sphere the field is **radial**: lines point straight in towards the centre.
Near the surface of a planet the lines are almost parallel and equally spaced, so the field is **uniform**.
A gravitational field is a region where a mass feels a force.
g = F/m is the force per unit mass, in N/kg.
Field lines point towards the mass; closer lines mean a stronger field.

blocks.text: Every mass attracts every other mass. Newton's law gives the size of that force between two point masses.

blocks.label: Newton's law of gravitation
where: F = gravitational force between the masses (N)
G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)

items: The force is proportional to the **product of the masses**.
The force is inversely proportional to the **square of the distance**: double r and F falls to a quarter.
The two masses pull on each other with equal and opposite forces.

blocks.text: The law is for point masses. A uniform sphere acts as if all its mass were at its centre, for any point outside it, so r is measured from the centre.

items: F = Gm₁m₂/r²: an inverse-square law, always attractive.
r is the distance between the centres of the masses.
A uniform sphere acts as a point mass at its centre.

sections.heading: Field strength of a point mass

blocks.text: Combining the definition of g with Newton's law gives the field strength at distance r from a point mass M.

items.text: Place a small test mass m at distance r from the mass M.
Use g = F/m, so g = (GMm/r²) ÷ m.
The test mass m cancels, leaving g = GM/r².

blocks.label: Field strength of a point mass
where: G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
r = distance from the centre of M (m)

diagram.question: A planet has mass {M} × 10²⁴ kg and radius {r} × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)

items: The Earth's radius is about 6400 km, so a change in height of a few kilometres changes r by a tiny fraction.
Then g = GM/r² hardly changes, so g is approximately constant at about 9.8 N/kg.
This field strength is numerically equal to the acceleration of free fall.
g = GM/r² for a point mass, or for a uniform sphere outside it.
g falls as 1/r²: double the distance and g falls to a quarter.
Near the surface g is approximately constant, as small height changes barely change r.

checks.a: The force per unit mass acting on a small test mass at that point (g = F/m).

checks.q: Two point masses are a distance r apart. State what happens to the force between them when the distance is tripled and one mass is doubled.
checks.a: F is proportional to m₁m₂/r². Doubling a mass doubles F; tripling r divides it by 9. The force becomes 2/9 of its original value.

checks.q: Derive g = GM/r² for the field strength at distance r from a point mass M.
checks.a: Force on a test mass m is F = GMm/r². Field strength is force per unit mass, g = F/m. Substituting and cancelling m gives g = GM/r².

blocks.text: Force fields arise from the interaction of mass, of static charge, and between moving charges. The direction of a field vector must be worked out by inspection.

items: Similarity: both gravitational and electrostatic forces have inverse-square laws, with field lines, the potential concept and equipotential surfaces.
Difference: masses always attract, but charges may attract or repel.

blocks.text: OCR writes the law with a minus sign. The sign shows that the force and the field point towards the mass, in the direction of decreasing r.

blocks.label: Signed forms
where: The negative sign means attraction: the vector points inwards

blocks.text: Gravitational fields are one of several forms of field that give rise to a force. Electric fields are another, and they are compared later.
